\title{Moved, Archived, Gone: How Often Widely Used Packages Lose Their
Upstream, and Whether Dependency Tools Can Tell}

\author{Mehmet Kış\\
Ikarus AI Labs, Cambridge, United Kingdom\\
\href{mailto:mehmet@ikaruslabs.net}{\texttt{mehmet@ikaruslabs.net}}}

\date{Draft, \today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent\textbf{Context.} Dependency tools decide whether a dependency
is safe mostly from vulnerability advisories and lifecycle catalogues.
Changes to the dependency's upstream, such as an archived, relocated or
deleted source repository, need not appear in either.
\textbf{Objective.} We measure how often the most depended-upon packages
of npm, PyPI and Go have such a change, how many dependents they have,
and whether the change is visible through a machine-readable signal a
dependency tool could act on.
\textbf{Method.} A pre-specified cross-sectional study of
\val{N} packages, the top 1,000 and a random 1,000 from ranks
1,001--20,000 per ecosystem, measuring each package's published source
repository through the GitHub API and its registry, advisory and
lifecycle records through their primary sources.
\textbf{Results.} Among the top 1,000 packages, \val{npm-top-any}\%
(npm), \val{pypi-top-any}\% (PyPI) and \val{go-top-any}\% (Go) have a
source repository that is archived, relocated or unreachable; in the
random sample from lower ranks, \val{npm-tail-any}\%, \val{pypi-tail-any}\%
and \val{go-tail-any}\%. The median archived npm package among the top
1,000 has \val{npm-top-archived-median-repos} dependent repositories. For archived
repositories, the registry's deprecation flag is the only signal with
material coverage, from \val{npm-top-archived-registry}\% (npm, top) down
to \val{go-tail-archived-registry}\% (Go, lower ranks); OSV and
endoflife.date matched at most \val{other-signal-max} package in any
ecosystem and stratum. Among repositories with a recorded earlier name,
the registry still publishes an earlier name for
\val{npm-top-stale}--\val{go-top-stale}\% of top packages and
\val{npm-tail-stale}--\val{pypi-tail-stale}\% of the others.
\textbf{Conclusion.} Upstream source changes are common among widely
used packages, and the advisory and lifecycle data dependency tools read
almost never record them; a tool that wants to see them has to ask the
source host.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

% Motivation: advisories (OSV, GHSA) and lifecycle data (endoflife.date)
% cover vulnerabilities and announced support windows. Repository-level
% changes - archival, transfer, deletion - change who can fix the code and
% where it lives, without necessarily producing either kind of record.
% Examples from TR-2026-01 (etcd relocation, Bitnami withdrawal) are
% anecdotes; this paper measures the phenomenon.

\paragraph{Research questions.}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,label=RQ\arabic*.]
  \item \emph{Prevalence.} Among the most depended-upon packages of npm,
    PyPI and Go, what share have a source repository that is archived,
    relocated, or no longer reachable?
  \item \emph{Exposure.} How many dependent packages and repositories do
    those packages have?
  \item \emph{Signal coverage.} For packages whose source repository is
    archived or unreachable, what share carry a registry deprecation
    flag, an OSV advisory, or an endoflife.date entry?
  \item \emph{Stale references.} Among packages whose source repository
    has a recorded earlier name, what share of registry metadata still
    publishes an earlier name, so that consumers reach the code only
    through a platform redirect?
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
  \item A measurement of upstream source changes across three
    ecosystems, separated into strata so that it is not read as
    ecosystem-wide.
  \item A measurement of how much of it is visible to tools that read
    registries, advisories and lifecycle data.
  \item A replication package: the frozen sample, every raw response,
    the collector and the analysis.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
All \val{N} sampled packages were measured; no GitHub request ended in an
error. Results are per ecosystem and stratum and are never pooled. Every
percentage carries a Wilson 95\% interval in brackets. The full output of
the pre-specified analysis, including counts per distinct repository, is
\code{data/main/RESULTS.md} in the replication package.

\subsection{RQ1: Prevalence}

Table~\ref{tab:rq1} gives the share of measured packages in each state.
Packages whose registry metadata publishes no GitHub repository are
excluded (column \emph{Excl.}); exclusion is highest on PyPI
(\val{pypi-top-excluded} of the top 1,000 and \val{pypi-tail-excluded}
of the lower-ranked sample), so PyPI results describe the packages that
publish a GitHub repository, not all of PyPI.

Archived is the most common state in every group, from
\val{npm-top-archived}\% of top npm packages to \val{go-tail-archived}\%
of lower-ranked Go modules. In every ecosystem the lower-ranked sample has
a higher point estimate in each state than the top 1,000 (for archived Go
modules, \val{go-tail-archived}\% against \val{go-top-archived}\%, with
overlapping intervals), and unreachable
repositories are rare among top packages (\val{pypi-top-unreachable}--%
\val{go-top-unreachable}\%) but reach \val{npm-tail-unreachable}--%
\val{go-tail-unreachable}\% below them. These are descriptions; the study
tests no difference.

\subsection{RQ2: Exposure}

Table~\ref{tab:rq2} gives the number of dependent repositories of the
affected packages, as reported by ecosyste.ms. Dependent counts overlap
across packages (one project depends on many), so they are given as
medians and maxima and are never summed into a count of affected
projects. Exposure follows rank: the median archived npm package among
the top 1,000 has \val{npm-top-archived-median-repos} dependent
repositories, against \val{pypi-top-archived-median-repos} on PyPI and
\val{go-top-archived-median-repos} on Go; below the top 1,000 the medians
fall to \val{npm-tail-archived-median-repos},
\val{pypi-tail-archived-median-repos} and
\val{go-tail-archived-median-repos}. The dependent counts of the three
ecosystems are not comparable with each other, because each registry
records dependents differently.

\subsection{RQ3: Signal coverage}

Table~\ref{tab:rq3} gives, for archived and unreachable packages, the
share that carries each machine-readable signal. Almost all coverage
comes from the registry's own deprecation flag, and it differs by
ecosystem: \val{npm-top-archived-registry}\% of archived top npm
packages are deprecated on npm, against \val{go-top-archived-registry}\%
on Go and \val{pypi-top-archived-registry}\% on PyPI, and fewer below the
top 1,000. OSV advisories and endoflife.date entries matched at most
\val{other-signal-max} archived or unreachable package in any ecosystem
and stratum. For unreachable repositories the groups are small (as few as
one package) and the intervals wide.

These figures rest on lexical matching (Section~\ref{sec:threats}); the
human validation of the matched and unmatched signals is reported in
Section~\ref{sec:validation}.

\subsection{Archived but still released}

The protocol (§5) records whether an archived package had a release after
its repository's last push, as a proxy for development having moved
elsewhere. This holds for \val{npm-top-archived-released}\% of archived
top npm packages, \val{pypi-top-archived-released}\% on PyPI and
\val{go-top-archived-released}\% on Go (below the top 1,000:
\val{npm-tail-archived-released}\%, \val{pypi-tail-archived-released}\%
and \val{go-tail-archived-released}\%). Most archived packages, in other
words, have had no release since their repository stopped changing. The
proxy does not tell \emph{moved} from \emph{abandoned}; the rating of
archived repositories (Section~\ref{sec:validation}) does.

\subsection{Validation}
\label{sec:validation}

\paragraph{Frame against source.} The ecosyste.ms \code{archived} flag
agrees with the GitHub measurement for \val{frame-agree}\% of the
\val{frame-n} packages where both exist. The protocol named a random 10\%
sample for this check; the analysis compares every package, which
contains any such sample. GitHub decides every result regardless.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
% Implications for dependency tools and SBOM producers; for registries
% (publishing repository state); for agents choosing dependencies.

\section{Threats to Validity}
\label{sec:threats}
\paragraph{Construct validity.} Archived is not abandoned; unreachable
includes private repositories; lexical signal matching (estimated in the
validation sample).
\paragraph{Internal validity.} The study is descriptive and draws no
causal conclusion. Ecosyste.ms decides only the frame and the ranking;
the frame-versus-source agreement is reported.
\paragraph{External validity.} Three ecosystems, GitHub-hosted sources
only, a ranked frame; the \emph{Tail} stratum limits but does not remove
the bias towards popular packages.
\paragraph{Conclusion validity.} Proportions with intervals and no
hypothesis tests; overlapping dependent counts are never summed into a
count of affected projects.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
Among the most depended-upon packages of npm, PyPI and Go, between
\val{npm-top-any}\% and \val{go-top-any}\% of the top 1,000 have a source
repository that is archived, relocated or unreachable, and more of those
below them. The signals dependency tools usually read record little of
it: the registry's deprecation flag covers a share of archived packages
that varies widely by ecosystem, and advisory and lifecycle data almost
none. Registry metadata also keeps pointing at earlier repository names.
A dependency tool that is to see these changes cannot wait for an
advisory; it has to read the source host's own state.
\result{revise after the validation ratings (Section~\ref{sec:validation})}
